headline: In Alaska, Outside money tilted Democratic, and Kreiss-Tomkins leads for governor
dek: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and the groups backing him outraised and outspent the Republicans in Alaska's governor race, with his campaign drawing much of its money from California and New York. He leads on first choices, but the ranked-choice count is still to come.
summary: Democratic money, much from Outside, outweighed Republican money in Alaska's governor race; Kreiss-Tomkins leads 49-29 on first choices, uncalled.

paras.text: Alaska elected its governor on Nov. 3 to replace outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a term-limited Republican who has been governor since 2018. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democrat, leads Republican Bernadette Wilson by 103,837 to 61,734 first-choice votes. That is a margin of 19.9 points, in a state President Trump carried by 13.8 points in 2024. The Associated Press has not called the race. This is a state race, so the money behind it is reported to the Alaska Public Offices Commission, not the Federal Election Commission. The figures below come from those state filings, as reported by Alaska news outlets.

Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from Sitka, reported raising over $5.3 million since launching his campaign, far more than his three Republican opponents combined. In an October analysis, Alaska Public Media found that about 70% of Kreiss-Tomkins' campaign donations to date have come from out of state, and nearly half from donors with New York and California addresses. Early on, his top contributors include six employees of Anthropic, a California-based artificial intelligence company, who collectively gave Kreiss-Tomkins $372,000. (The Watch is written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic.) The Anchorage Daily News reported that since the primary, however, Kreiss-Tomkins appears to have steered clear of contributors affiliated with the AI industry. The campaign has also said he also brought in more money from more in-state donors than the rest of the field combined.

Wilson, a Republican who owns Denali Disposal, a trash-hauling company, raised far less. By late October she raised nearly $345,000 since the beginning of the month, bringing her campaign total to $1.5 million. Most of her donations were small and came from outside Alaska. Her largest recent contributor was Michael Parker, a Texan who gave her $50,000. Parker serves as board chair for Narwhal Exploration, an oil company preparing to search for oil off the North Slope. Former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson's campaign total stood at $440,000.

The national governors' associations put money into independent expenditure groups, Alaska's version of super PACs, which cannot coordinate with candidates. The Democratic Governors Association's contributions to Forward Frontier totaled $1.25 million, and the group also took money from a group called Democratic Action and the public employee union AFSCME. In response, the Republican Governors Association donated some $1.6 million to a new group in late September called Kodiak PAC. Kodiak PAC was registered by Casey Phillips, a Virginia-based consultant.

Forward Frontier was the biggest outside spender in the race. It has spent $4.4 million backing Kreiss-Tomkins, including $2.9 million in this month alone, according to the Daily News's Oct. 28 count. One of its ads, "Bring Together," opened on gas prices above $5 a gallon and a 30% jump in heating fuel costs. It then presented Kreiss-Tomkins as the candidate who would bring the parties together on costs, fisheries and data centers. A labor-affiliated group, Putting Alaskans First, reported spending $175,000 this week on radio ads intended to benefit Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.

On the Republican side, Kodiak PAC, a group funded by the Republican Governors Association, has spent $1.7 million backing the GOP candidates and opposing Kreiss-Tomkins. The group has not sought to differentiate between the Republicans. Another group, "Bernadette Will Build the Damn Roads," recently spent $98,000 on advertising to promote her. The group is funded primarily by a Florida-based private prison company called the GEO Group, which operates immigration detention facilities in the Lower 48.

Wilson's own campaign went after the Democrat's donors. In early October she ran an ad in recent days referring to Kreiss-Tomkins as "Chat-JKT," a play on the name of a popular AI platform and the candidate's initials. Republicans also derided Kreiss-Tomkins as "Just Keep Taxing," a play on his initials, over his plan to expand corporate income taxes on oil producers and a 2017 vote in support of a statewide personal income tax. In the last days, as Kreiss-Tomkins drove to Deadhorse on the Arctic Ocean, a campaign blimp with his initials flew over Midtown Anchorage.

The U.S. Senate race drew much more money. The Watch's own reading of the FEC data for Alaska is not finished, so these figures come from the press. Citing OpenSecrets, the Fairbanks Daily News-Miner reported that more than $138 million has been spent on Alaska's Senate race alone, including $43.5 million by the campaigns and $94.6 million by outside groups. Ads paid for by the Senate Leadership Fund, the leading Republican super PAC, said Democrat Mary Peltola "sold Alaska out". Some outside money also went to a long-shot candidate, with ads that encouraged voters to rank only Heikes on their ballot.

Kreiss-Tomkins and his allies spent much more than the Republicans, and he is ahead. But the race is not over. He has 49.1 % of first choices, short of a majority. That means Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation, which eliminates the last-place candidate round by round, will decide it. A preliminary tally by FairVote, an organization that advocates for ranked-choice voting, leads the race for governor 55%-45%, with his margin shrinking about 9.5 points in the RCV count. That tally used incomplete ballot data. If his lead holds, he would be Alaska's first Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002. The winner is set to take office at noon Dec. 7.

The money explains only part of the result. Before the vote, the Daily News described a weak Republican field: Wilson has been repeatedly sued over unpaid business and personal debts; Bronson was voted out of office after his one term as Anchorage mayor, and Treg Taylor was briefly kicked off the ballot over a disclosure filing. Wilson called her two Republican rivals "spoilers", and the three never united behind one candidate. In the Senate race, where outside money was close to even, Peltola leads Sullivan by 637 votes, and that race is also uncalled.
